title: Bounded, or totally bounded?

prereqs.why: The definition - finitely many balls of every radius - is what each line has to be tested against.
Bounded is the weaker condition the question is separating total boundedness from.
One of the five lives in a sequence space, where the two conditions come apart most dramatically.

statement:
A set $E$ in a metric space is **totally bounded** when, for every
$\eps > 0$, finitely many balls of radius $\eps$ cover $E$.

It is **bounded** when some single ball contains it.

Total boundedness implies boundedness and the converse fails. Select every
set below that is **totally bounded**.
hints: Boundedness is about one ball of some radius; total boundedness is about finitely many balls of every radius. Only the second is being asked for.
In the discrete metric a ball of radius $\tfrac12$ is a single point. How many of those does it take to cover an infinite set?

In $\ell^2$, the standard basis vectors $e_1, e_2, e_3, \dots$ all lie in the closed unit ball, and $d_2(e_i, e_j) = \sqrt2$ whenever $i \ne j$. How many of them can one ball of radius $\tfrac12$ hold?
In $\R^n$ there is a theorem: totally bounded and bounded are the same condition. Two of the five live in $\R^n$.
